new_entities.name: Anti-androgenic combined oral contraceptives
new_entities.description: Combined oral contraceptives with anti-androgenic properties used for acne control in women.

new_entities.name: Moderate acne in women
new_entities.description: Moderate acne vulgaris in female patients.

edges.effect_quant: In a pooled placebo-controlled analysis of 893 women, an ethinylestradiol 20 μg/drospirenone 3 mg regimen tripled the odds of investigator-rated clear or almost clear skin (OR 3.41, 95% CI 2.15 to 5.43). Placebo-controlled truncal and facial acne trials show the same direction of benefit.
edges.population: adolescent and adult women with moderate acne vulgaris using anti-androgenic combined oral contraceptive regimens
edges.mechanism: Anti-androgenic oral contraceptives reduce ovarian androgen signaling and sebaceous stimulation, which can lower lesion formation in hormonally responsive acne.
edges.summary: Anti-androgenic combined oral contraceptives are a real acne intervention, not just a side effect of contraception. The clinical-trial literature shows consistent lesion reduction and higher odds of clear or almost clear skin in women with moderate acne.
edges.caveats: This edge is limited to women who are appropriate candidates for combined hormonal contraception. It should be interpreted alongside contraceptive risks and preferences rather than as a universally interchangeable acne medication.

evidence.citation: KoltunW et al 2011 Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol
evidence.notes: Treatment of moderate acne vulgaris using a combined oral contraceptive containing ethinylestradiol 20 μg plus drospirenone 3mg administered in a 24/4 regimen: a pooled analysis.

effect_quant.comparator: investigator-rated clear or almost clear skin with EE/drospirenone versus placebo

evidence.citation: MaloneyJM et al 2009 J Drugs Dermatol
evidence.notes: A randomized controlled trial of a low-dose combined oral contraceptive containing 3 mg drospirenone plus 20 microg ethinylestradiol in the treatment of acne vulgaris: lesion counts, investigator ratings and subject self-assessment.
